alignment.note: καί / ܘ- / et — coordinating conjunction; in Syriac the waw is prefixed to the verb.
καθεύδω / root n-d-m (ܘܢܕܡܟ) / dormiat — 'sleep'; the Syriac form fuses the conjunction and verb into a single graphic unit.
καί / et — second coordinating conjunction; the Syriac again prefixes the waw to the following verb rather than supplying a separate token.

Greek ἐγείρηται (passive/middle of ἐγείρω, 'be raised/wake') and Vulgate exsurgat ('rise up') are both rendered by Syriac ܘܢܩܘܡ from root q-w-m ('arise, stand'); the Syriac and Latin foreground the act of rising while the Greek middle nuances waking.
νύκτα / ܒܠܠܝܐ / nocte — 'night'; Syriac and Latin mark the temporal phrase prepositionally/by case (Syriac ܒ-, Latin ablative), whereas Greek uses the accusative of duration.
καί / ܘ- (prefixed) / et — conjunction joining the temporal pair; Syriac fuses the waw to ܐܝܡܡܐ.
ἡμέραν / ܒܐܝܡܡܐ (root y-m-m) / die — 'day'; Syriac again prefixes ܒ- to mark the temporal sense, matching the Latin ablative against the Greek accusative.
καί / ܘ- (prefixed to ܙܪܥܐ) / et — conjunction introducing the seed clause.

Greek supplies the article ὁ σπόρος ('the seed') as a definite subject; Latin semen and Syriac ܙܪܥܐ render the noun without a separate article, the Syriac emphatic state and the Latin anarthrous noun both functioning as the subject.

Greek βλαστᾷ ('sprout, germinate') is matched closely by Latin germinet; the Syriac ܢܪܒܐ (root denoting 'grow great/increase') stresses growth in size rather than the act of sprouting, a slight semantic shift toward the following verb.
καί / ܘ- (prefixed to ܢܐܪܟ) / et — conjunction joining the two growth verbs.

Greek μηκύνηται ('lengthen, become tall') is rendered by Syriac ܢܐܪܟ, which likewise denotes lengthening/growing tall and is the natural cognate sense; Latin increscat ('increase') generalises to overall growth rather than specifically height.

Greek ὡς introduces a manner/comparative clause ('how/in a way that'); Syriac ܟܕ and Latin dum are temporal-circumstantial subordinators ('while/as'), yielding a slightly different syntactic framing of the farmer's ignorance.
οὐκ / ܠܐ / nescit (negation incorporated into the Latin verb) — negative particle; Latin fuses the negation into nescit ('does not know').
οἶδεν / ܝܕܥ (root y-d-ʿ) / (ne-)scit — 'knows'; the Latin negative verb nescit subsumes both the verb and its negation in one form.
αὐτός / ܗܘ / ille — emphatic third-person subject pronoun reinforcing the agent's ignorance; word order varies (Greek final, Syriac preceding the negation, Latin final).
